problem.title: A PDF remembers how a page looks. Not what the content means.
problem.lede: PDF (Portable Document Format) was built to save and exchange electronic documents so they look the same on every device, in every app. That is a feature when you need a contract, a report, or a printed handbook. It is a problem when you need the content.
problem.quote: A PDF is saving “how this document should look,” not “what this document is made of.”
problem.goodTag: What a PDF is good at
problem.badH: Hard for work — and for AI
problem.goodRows[0].means: Fonts, images, tables, spacing, headers, and footers stay put. The page does not reflow when you change devices.
problem.goodRows[1].means: Windows, macOS, Linux, iOS, and Android can all open it.
problem.goodRows[2].means: Page size and print layout hold up, which is why contracts, reports, papers, and manuals ship as PDF.
problem.goodRows[3].means: Once generated, it works as a final version: read it, share it, archive it.
problem.goodRows[4].means: A PDF is rarely “just text.” It may include images, tables, links, vector graphics, embedded fonts, and scanned pages.
problem.badRows[0].hurts: PDF cares about the page, not the outline. Machines struggle to recover headings, paragraphs, lists, and tables.
problem.badRows[1].hurts: Unlike Word or Markdown, PDF was not designed for frequent rewriting or reorganization.
problem.badRows[2].hurts: Embedded fonts, multi-column layouts, tables, images, and footnotes all make extraction harder.
problem.badRows[3].hurts: Many PDFs are scans — images of pages. You need OCR before you can even get the words.
problem.seeP: On the page, a PDF might look like a chapter, a section, a list, a table.

problem.softP: A program often sees something else: strings, coordinates, fonts, and images scattered across a canvas. Recovering the real title, the paragraph boundaries, the list, and the table is not guaranteed.
problem.gap1: PDF is for humans. It emphasizes visual layout.
problem.gap2: Markdown is for structured content — editing, software, and AI.
problem.gap3: Once you have Markdown, the same document is ready for search, knowledge bases, RAG, embeddings, and LLMs.
problem.close: Dropping a PDF straight into a knowledge base is often the wrong first step. The model may get text. It does not get structure.
md.title: Markdown keeps the content. And makes the structure explicit.
md.lede: Markdown is a lightweight markup language. A few plain-text symbols stand in for headings, paragraphs, lists, tables, links, and code. You can read the source without rendering it.

intent.title: Scans, tables, RAG, chat windows, and whole folders.
intent.lede: These sit next to the main query. Each is a job the file has to survive — not another lecture on formats.
intents[0].p: A scanned handbook is a stack of images. There is no text layer until OCR runs — and OCR alone still leaves a stream of characters. The useful path is OCR plus structure: reading order, heading levels, and tables rebuilt as tables, not as a photograph of a grid. That is how a scan becomes something you can search, chunk, or edit. Contracts, invoices, and older papers are often scans; born-digital files can skip OCR, scans cannot skip the outline. Low-contrast stamps, skewed pages, and mixed handwriting still fail and need a second look. If you index the OCR dump as-is, a knowledge base stores noise.
intents[1].h: Structured files for RAG and embeddings
intents[1].p: When you embed a PDF as-is, the splitter often cuts mid-table or mid-section because it never saw a heading. Retrieval then returns a blob that looks related and is not. Give the pipeline Markdown with explicit headings and real tables, and chunking can follow the outline: one section, one table, one list. Embeddings stay closer to a single topic. That is the data-prep job — not a nicer preview. You still choose chunk size, overlap, and the vector store; conversion does not replace that. It stops the model from embedding headers, footers, and page numbers as if they were the answer.
intents[2].p: Copy-paste and naive extractors flatten a two-column report into one stream: the heading is just larger type, the table is leftover spaces. Downstream you cannot sort a column or retrieve “section 4.2.” Conversion should emit Markdown headings and pipe tables, with reading order that matches how a person would read the page — including multi-column layouts when they exist. Footnotes and captions should stay attached to the block they belong to. If a table was a screenshot, OCR has to run on that image or the grid is lost. The test is simple: can you jump the outline, and can you copy a row?
intents[3].p: Pasting pages into ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini is fine for a one-off summary. It is a weak plan for a library. The model gets a weakly ordered blob; headings and tables are guesses. You cannot version the source, re-chunk it, or hand a clean file to the rest of the team. Convert first, then prompt: the outline sits in the file, figures stay in tables, and the same Markdown can go to another model, an internal RAG, or Git. Use the chat window to ask questions. Do not use it as your only extractor — especially not for a 100-page report you will query again next month.
intents[4].p: One file is a demo. Operations look like a folder: two hundred manuals, a contract archive, a paper corpus. Batch conversion should keep filenames, skip files that already have a .md, and fail visibly when a scan needs OCR or a table collapsed. Put output next to the original — or in a parallel tree — so you can diff and re-run. After that, the same corpus can be indexed, embedded, or published without someone opening each PDF. Start with a sample of ugly files (multi-column, scans, mixed tables) before you point the job at everything.
faq.title: Questions worth answering before you convert.
faqs[0].q: Is there a Python library or pip package?
faqs[0].a: This site is a browser-based converter, not a pip module. For quick one-file jobs, use the tool above. For fully programmatic pipelines, common libraries include PyMuPDF, pdfplumber and marker — or wait for our upcoming API.
faqs[1].q: Can I use the output in Jupyter or pandas?
faqs[1].a: Yes. Copy the Markdown into a notebook cell for documentation, or parse GFM tables into DataFrames with pandas.read_table on the table blocks.
faqs[2].q: Does this replace a Python script in production?
faqs[2].a: For ad-hoc and prototype work, the browser tool is faster to start. For automated batch jobs in CI or cron, a script or API is better — our API is planned for that use case.
faqs[3].q: Why is OCR slower than a normal conversion?
faqs[3].a: OCR analyzes each page image pixel by pixel to recognize characters, which is heavier than reading an existing text layer. Larger documents take longer.
faqs[4].q: Will multi-column layouts, footnotes, embedded fonts, and mixed tables survive?
faqs[4].a: Those are the hard cases — and they are common. They are also why a dedicated PDF → Markdown step exists. A conversion that only concatenates strings will scramble reading order and miss the outline.
faqs[5].q: Is this for one file or a whole archive?
faqs[5].a: Both. One report, so you can ask an LLM about it. A thousand manuals, SOPs, and training PDFs, so you can chunk, embed, and retrieve. Use the batch converter for folders. The product is the prep step either way — and it stays local.
faqs[6].q: Do I still need the original PDF?
faqs[6].a: Yes, when you need a stable, print-faithful, shareable original. Conversion does not replace PDF for contracts, invoices, or archival copies. It unlocks a second life for the same content.
faqs[7].q: Can I turn the Markdown back into a site or other formats?
faqs[7].a: That is one of the reasons to convert. Markdown is easy to turn into HTML, PDF, Word, docs sites, FAQs, blog posts, and AI datasets. The PDF was a download. The Markdown is a source.

sections[5].title: 6. Data sharing
sections[5].paragraphs[0]: We do not sell your personal information. Usage data collected by Google Analytics and Microsoft Clarity is shared with those respective providers as described in their privacy policies.
sections[5].paragraphs[1]: We may also disclose information if required by law, court order, or to protect the rights, property, or safety of our users or the public.
sections[6].title: 7. Data retention
sections[6].paragraphs[0]: Analytics data is retained according to the retention policies of Google Analytics and Microsoft Clarity. PDF files and conversion output are never stored on our servers.
sections[7].title: 8. Your rights and choices
sections[7].paragraphs[0]: Depending on your location, you may have rights to access, correct, or delete personal data held about you. You can also:
sections[7].bullets[0]: Opt out of Google Analytics using the browser add-on linked above
sections[7].bullets[1]: Block or delete cookies via your browser settings
sections[7].bullets[2]: Use a privacy-focused browser or extensions to limit tracking
sections[8].title: 9. Children's privacy
sections[8].paragraphs[0]: Our service is not directed at children under 13. We do not knowingly collect personal information from children.
sections[9].title: 10. Changes to this policy
sections[9].paragraphs[0]: We may update this Privacy Policy from time to time. When we do, we will revise the "Last updated" date at the top of this page. Continued use of the site after changes constitutes acceptance of the updated policy.
